name: Sketch Pencil 14 Pose
notes:
BRIEF. sketch-pencil.json with the worn graphite modelled: same mechanical-pencil line and the same tonal range, with the facet bound to the pen's pose instead of to the canvas and the paper tooth subtracted rather than multiplied. A stroke pulled along the barrel comes out a fine dark line; the same stroke pulled across it comes out broad and lighter, and the difference follows the hand rather than the page. Everything else in sketch-pencil's brief still applies and is unchanged here.

THE GEOMETRY. A used lead is a cylinder cut off at the angle it is held at, so the patch touching the paper is an ellipse: its SHORT axis is the lead diameter, its LONG axis is diameter/cos(grip), and the long axis lies along the barrel's shadow on the page — the projection of the pencil onto the paper. Sweep the pencil along that long axis and the mark is one lead wide. Sweep it across and the mark is the whole facet. That is the whole effect, and it is three settings: tip.angle bound to Pen Tilt, which in this engine (and in Photoshop's bVTy 3) rotates the tip to the tilt AZIMUTH — the direction the pen leans — a tip.roundness under 1 to give the ellipse something to be narrow about, and tip.angle at 90 to undo the quarter turn Photoshop applies (see CONFIRMED IN PHOTOSHOP below).

SIZE IS THE LONG AXIS, WHICH IS WHY 14 BECAME 40. The engine parameterises an elliptical tip by its long axis and squashes the short one by roundness, so a 14px tip at roundness 0.35 draws a 14px facet with a 5px lead — a much thinner pencil, not a worn one. The lead is the thing that must not move: at roundness 0.35 the size that keeps it is 14/0.35 = 40px. Measured, that holds the along-the-barrel line at the current brush's 10px through every facet depth swept, and lets the across-the-barrel mark grow instead. The panel now says 40px for a pencil that still draws a 10px line; that is the parameterisation, not a resize. Resizing still works: both axes scale together, so the ratio holds.

TEXTURE SCALE, AND WHY IT IS 0.5 AND NOT 0.4. sketch-pencil's note says to rescale texture.scale alongside tip.size. It does not apply here, because the physical lead did not change size — only the number the engine calls Size did. The tooth sits at 0.5 of a 512px pattern, a 256px tile carrying 2.4-6.5px grain on canvas — several cycles across the 10px line, the ratio sketch-pencil settled on, reached by designing the band rather than by scaling a bitmap that happened to contain it.

WHAT THE MEASUREMENTS SETTLED. The pose fan, at 0/30/60/90/120/150 degrees off the barrel with the pen laid over 45: 10/17/25/29/25/17px, 2.9x wide-to-narrow, and the probe confirms it turns with the pen rather than sitting on the canvas. The current brush measures 10/11/11/11/9/9px, 1.22x, fixed to the canvas — that 1.22x is its 35-degree facet caught side-on, and it is why the effect was never felt in the hand: it was there, but it was pinned to the page. Note that the along-the-barrel width is 10px in both, and stays 10px at every facet depth. That is the design: the everyday line is the line this brush already had, and what the pose adds is the broad mark, not a thinner one. Both renderers agree on the fan to the pixel.

TONE CARRIED OVER, MEASURED WHERE THE TWO CAN BE COMPARED. `measure` scales its own probe surface with tip size, so its flat-stroke numbers for a 14px brush and a 40px brush are not read off the same geometry; these were taken on one surface at one y, both brushes, stroke along the barrel. Peak alpha of the fine line up the pressure ladder: 0.24/0.58/0.73/0.80/0.85 at 10/30/50/70/100%, against the current brush's 0.24/0.55/0.71/0.78/0.85 — the same curve. Build-up over 1/2/4 passes runs 0.617/0.834/0.949 (x1.35/x1.54) against the current brush's 0.535/0.728/0.843 (x1.36/x1.58): the working-in headroom the 0.60 draft had lost came back when the texture went to subtract, which takes ink out of the first pass rather than scaling it.

DO NOT TUNE THIS BRUSH AGAINST `measure`'s GRAIN NUMBER. It reads 0.102 here and 0.42 for the current brush, and neither is the paper tooth: for a mark this narrow the flat probe's band statistics are dominated by whether the two soft edge rows clear the 8/255 ink floor, which flips on a fraction of a pixel of tip size — an earlier draft of this brush measured 0.09 at 23px and 0.43 at 23.3px, same settings otherwise. Grain measured across a broad sweep at a fixed geometry, light pressure against heavy, is the honest test; that is the pair quoted under the tooth below.

FACET DEPTH IS A TOOL DECISION, NOT A PHYSICAL ONE. roundness = cos(grip), so read as geometry the number is a grip angle: 0.75 is a 41-degree hold, 0.60 is 53, 0.35 is 70. Swept with size set to 14/roundness each time so the lead stays put, anisotropy runs 1.8x / 2.2x / 2.5x / 3.1x / 3.6x / 4.3x for 0.60/0.50/0.42/0.35/0.30/0.25, the along-the-barrel line holds at 10px and peak 0.83 throughout, and nothing gaps anywhere — the depth is free of every other part of the design, which is what makes it a dial rather than a trade.

0.60 was the first draft and it was judged too quiet in review. 0.35 is what replaced it: a 10px line against a 29px sweep. Read as a grip that is 70 degrees, further over than anyone holds a mechanical pencil, so this is past the point where the geometry is the reason — it is the effect the hand wants, and the geometry only says which axis it goes on. The broad mark does lighten as the facet deepens (peak 0.73 at 0.60, 0.61 at 0.35, 0.52 at 0.25) because the dabs overlap less across the short axis; 0.30 and 0.25 are on the shelf if it should be louder still, at the cost of a sweep that cannot be worked as dark.

THE TOOTH IS SUBTRACTED, NOT MULTIPLIED. This is the second thing review changed, and it is the mode, not the depth. `multiply` scales the mark's alpha by the pattern, so the tooth is a fixed PROPORTION of whatever ink is there: it dims uniformly and never breaks anything up, which is why the old brush's texture read as a veil rather than as paper. `subtract` takes an ABSOLUTE bite instead, so the tooth wins wherever the ink is thin and loses wherever it is thick — a light pass breaks into the tooth's peaks, a heavy pass fills the valleys and goes solid. That is what dry media does, and it puts texture under the same finger that controls tone.

Measured on the broad sweep, grain against pressure: multiply at depth 0.4 gives 0.16 light / 0.14 heavy — flat, i.e. the tooth is doing the same thing however hard you press. subtract at 0.5 gives 0.24 light / 0.18 heavy. The fine line's pressure ladder is untouched by the choice (0.24/0.58/0.73/0.80/0.85 against multiply's 0.28/0.60/0.75/0.81/0.86), so the mode is free of the tonal design.

THE TOOTH IS ALSO NOT THE BUILT-IN ONE ANY MORE. Review's second complaint was a repeating pattern at large scales — shade a region and a grid of the same blotch appears. It is real, it is the texture tile, and the harness had already said so and been read past: `measure` reported a beat every 2.525 diameters standing 3316x above the noise floor, which is 101px, which is the 256px `paper` bitmap at scale 0.4. A canvas-registered texture tiles every native x scale px and there is no setting that stops it.

What stops it being VISIBLE is the pattern's own content. A tiled field's spectrum is the pattern's, sampled at multiples of 1/tile, so a repeat needs the pattern to carry something recognisable — and recognition needs a shape, which needs energy at a scale the eye can hold. `paper` carries 71% of its variance at canvas scales of 8px and coarser at this working scale: those are the blotches, and they land on the grid. `patterns/paper-tooth.png` is the same tooth with that half deleted — synthesized by tools/tile-pattern.mjs with a hard spectral floor at 6.5 canvas px, so every lattice line coarse enough to carry a motif is exactly zero rather than merely small. Its mean and standard deviation are matched to the built-in's (0.537 / 0.093) so the tone did not have to be retuned.

Measured on a shaded patch: coarse variance 71.2% to 0.0%, the patch's worst spectral spike 1,120,387x to 33x, splotchiness at stroke-width scale 2.8% to 0.1%, delivered texture contrast unchanged at 2.4%, tone 0.649 to 0.634. `measure`'s repetition row now reports no periodic line at all where it used to report 3316x. Raising `texture.scale` is NOT the alternative: it lengthens the tile and moves the coarse octaves up into view at the same time, so `paper` at 1.0 measures 96.8% coarse — worse than at 0.4.

WHAT THE NEW TOOTH COSTS. Paper's cloudiness IS low-frequency content, so a tooth that cannot repeat visibly also cannot be cloudy. This is even tooth, not handmade-paper mottle. That is the right trade for an under-drawing — the large-scale variation in a sketch should come from the hand, from pressure and overlap and where the strokes went, not from a bitmap that repeats every 256px — but it is a trade, and if mottle is wanted back it needs a mechanism that travels with the work rather than with the canvas. The pattern costs 259KB in the exported pack against 67KB for a built-in.

OTHER TEXTURE TREATMENTS, TRIED AND WHY THEY ARE NOT THIS ONE.
• `height` is `subtract` at 1.5x the depth; it erases the light sweep almost entirely before the heavy one has any grain. Use it if the tooth should be coarse and the light end should skip.
• `linear burn` behaves like subtract (0.24/0.19) but takes 16% of the ink against subtract's 12% at matched grain. Interchangeable; subtract is the shallower way to the same place.
• `darken` caps the mark at the tooth instead of biting into it, so the grain appears only once the mark is DARKER than the pattern — the inverse pressure response. Right for something that fills valleys first, backwards for graphite.
• `hard mix` is a binary threshold: maximum grain, no midtones, and the fine line turns into a solid slab. A frottage tool, not a pencil.
• `overlay` / `screen` / `lighten` / `color dodge` brighten the mark where the tooth is high, which reads as bleaching rather than as paper.
• `textureEachTip: true` gives each stamp its own sample of the pattern and unlocks depth jitter. At 5% spacing twenty stamps overlap per diameter, and twenty independent bites leave a patchy near-empty mark. It is a wide-spacing feature.
• `scale` at 1.0 turns `paper`'s coarse octave into blotches the size of the mark. 0.4 keeps the fine octave near 1.6px, which is the tooth.
• `speckle` instead of `paper` gives even, hard flecks at every pressure — cleaner and more uniform, and it is also the least repetitive built-in (19.9% of its variance coarse, against paper's 71.2%), which is the same reason. Without paper's clumping it reads as noise on the mark rather than as a surface under it. `canvas` is a visible woven grid and is simply a different material. `clouds` is 98.6% coarse and repeats worst of all.
• A Dual Brush gate (granite-grit, 12% spacing) does add breakup, but its mask travels with the stroke: it is the lead skipping, not the paper standing still, so overlapping strokes disagree about where the surface is. Costs render time too. Rejected for the same reason the first draft rejected it.
• Grain in the tip bitmap itself would rotate with the facet, which is right for something on the lead and wrong for something on the paper — and at 5% spacing twenty overlapping dabs average it away regardless.
• A bitmap of our own, declared as `patterns: { tooth: { image: "..." } }` and referenced as `@tooth`, is the route to a chosen spectrum. That is what this brush now does.

WHAT THE ENGINE CANNOT DO HERE, SO IT IS NOT ATTEMPTED.
• The facet cannot deepen as the pen is laid over. Physically roundness should fall as the grip angle rises (the cut through the cylinder gets longer), and every Control in this engine — Photoshop's included — ramps its parameter UP with the input: bound to Pen Tilt, roundness is FLATTEST upright and ROUNDEST laid over, which is backwards for a pencil and right for a chisel marker held on its corner. So the grip is a constant here (0.60, a 53-degree hold) rather than something the pen reports. Worth re-testing against Photoshop before assuming the engine is the one that is wrong: our tilt-roundness ramp is a linear 0-at-upright to 1-at-60, Photoshop stores a tiltScale next to it that we write at a fixed 200% and never read, and 200% is exactly what would make cos(2 x tilt) reach flat at 45 degrees. If Photoshop turns out to flatten with tilt, this brush wants roundnessControl on tilt and the engine wants fixing, in that order.
• At zero tilt the azimuth does not exist — atan2(0,0) is 0 — so a mouse, or a stylus held dead upright, gets a facet lying flat along the canvas x-axis. That is no worse than the fixed 35 degrees this replaces, but it does mean the brush is only itself under a pen that reports tilt. Every probe in `measure` except the pose fan paints at zero tilt, so their numbers describe this brush pulled ALONG its facet, which is the narrow dark case.

REJECTED, SO IT IS NOT RE-TRIED.
• Angle bound to Direction, or to Initial Direction. It is the obvious way to get a direction-dependent width and it is the wrong tool: direction-bound, the tip turns to follow the path, so the mark keeps ONE width through every turn — the exact opposite of what a facet does. The facet must stay still in canvas space while the stroke turns around it. Only pose sources (tilt, rotation) hold still.
• Barrel rotation (Rotation / twist) as a second input. Physically it is real — spinning the pencil turns the facet — but the wear tracks the habitual grip, so the facet follows the hand's lean much more than the barrel's spin, and hardly any tablet reports twist. Tilt alone is both the bigger effect and the one that gets reported.
• Shrinking the tip back to 14px and living with an 8px line. Tried in the sweep; it is a thinner pencil that happens to be anisotropic, not a worn one.

KNOWN TRADE, DEEPENED. sketch-pencil noted that a single dab peaks at 0.18 alpha, so stippling with taps is faint. Here it peaks at 0.13 and the plate's dab row is nearly bare below full pressure: the same flow is spread over a 40px stamp, and subtract then takes an absolute bite out of what is left. Scribbled tone is unaffected — that is strokes, where twenty dabs overlap — but this brush does not stipple. Raising flow would fix the taps and cost the tonal headroom, which is the trade sketch-pencil already made once.

CONFIRMED IN PHOTOSHOP, AND IT COST 90 DEGREES. The first export imported with the facet across the barrel instead of along it — the mark was right in the try-out app and wrong in Photoshop, which means the engines disagreed and Photoshop is the one that decides. Photoshop's Pen Tilt on an angle lays the tip's long axis ACROSS the lean: that is a flat nib's behaviour, since tilting foreshortens a disc along the lean and leaves it broadest across it, and it is a defensible thing for Adobe to have chosen. It is simply not what a worn pencil does. The engine now carries that quarter turn, so both programs agree, and `tip.angle: 90` here is what turns the facet back along the barrel. A nib brush would want 0.

The sign of the quarter turn is still open and this brush cannot settle it: an ellipse at +90 and -90 is the same ellipse. It will matter the first time a sampled tip that is not symmetric about its long axis is bound to tilt.
